edition.deck: A new round of US tariffs, a record run of global heat and fresh pressure on UK households lead the evening briefing.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises developments confirmed or sharpened during the day, alongside consequential continuing stories. The Russian casualty estimate returns because the fresh Danish analysis adds context and uncertainty to the earlier report.

content.headline: US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the EU
content.shortHeadline: US proposes tariffs on China, the EU and 12 other partners
content.standfirst: The proposed duties could take effect next year, with China facing rates of up to 40%. The European Commission says it will examine the move, while economists differ on how much it could raise prices.

image.caption: Donald Trump’s tariff policy targets imports from major US trading partners.

sources.originalTitle: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU
Dansk Industri: Amerikanerne bliver de store tabere, hvis Trump indfører endnu en straftold

segments.body: The US has set out proposed new import duties on 14 trading partners, including China, the EU, Japan and India. The rate for China could reach 40%; other partners face rates of up to 35%, 25% or 20%. The duties are not expected to take effect until next year.

segments.title: Costs and response
segments.body: The European Commission says it will investigate the US rationale and points to the 15% tariff ceiling previously agreed with Washington. Economists warn that businesses may pass higher costs on to consumers, though one analyst says the extra burden could be small. Dansk Industri likewise expects US consumers and companies to bear much of any added cost.

perspectives.body: Dansk Industri analyst Peter Bay Kierkegaard says Danish companies are unlikely to be badly affected because US buyers have so far been willing to pay more for European goods.

content.headline: Leaked Russian records suggest nearly 500,000 soldiers have died in Ukraine
content.shortHeadline: Leaked records suggest nearly 500,000 Russian war deaths
content.standfirst: BBC Russian’s analysis of leaked mortality records estimates that at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the 2022 invasion. The files are incomplete, and Russia has not published an official toll.

image.caption: Russia does not publish an updated official count of its military deaths.

sources.originalTitle: Russia's own figures show it has lost nearly 500,000 people in Ukraine war
Hvad betaler russerne for krigen i Ukraine? Et hackerangreb på russisk data har givet et bud

segments.body: BBC Russian analysed more than 11 million leaked Russian death records, cross-checking them with independent Russian outlet Mediazona’s list of confirmed military deaths. The analysis estimates at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the full-scale invasion began in 2022; the Kremlin says only the defence ministry should report official losses.

segments.title: A difficult count
segments.body: The estimate is not a complete tally. The BBC says military experts believe its own confirmed-deaths list may represent 45–55% of the true toll, while DR’s analysis describes other estimates that rise above 700,000 when missing soldiers are included. Some records may also include civilians or deaths from illness and accidents, and the data may be incomplete or delayed.

perspectives.body: DR’s analysis highlights the range of estimates: it reports that some counts exceed 700,000 when missing soldiers are included, while noting that the leaked records do not always distinguish combatants from civilians.

content.headline: Global temperatures stay above 2C over preindustrial levels for six days
content.shortHeadline: Global heat stays above 2C for six days in a row
content.standfirst: The latest daily reading reached 2.24C above the 1850–1900 average. Scientists say the brief record run does not mean the Paris temperature limit has been breached, but it underscores the effects of human-caused warming and a strong El Niño.

image.caption: A forest fire burns in Brazil’s Amazon region amid drought and rising global temperatures.

sources.originalTitle: World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time

segments.body: The world has recorded six consecutive days with average temperatures more than 2C above preindustrial levels for the first time, according to data reported by the Guardian. Monday’s daily reading was 2.24C above the 1850–1900 baseline, and the streak was forecast to continue.

segments.title: A warning, not a threshold verdict
segments.body: Scientists say a short run of hot days does not mean the Paris Agreement’s temperature limit has been breached. They attribute the readings to long-term human-caused warming alongside an unusually large El Niño, and warn that drought and fires can weaken tropical ecosystems’ ability to absorb carbon.

content.headline: Nvidia shares slide as Trump’s intervention in CEO’s return draws scrutiny
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia shares fall as Huang’s return faces renewed scrutiny
content.standfirst: Nvidia fell around 8% in New York trading after a sharp rebound tied to chief executive Jensen Huang’s return. The swing comes as lawmakers press questions about the company and President Donald Trump’s role.

image.caption: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s return has drawn political scrutiny in Washington.

sources.originalTitle: Teknologiaktier oplever store fald ved børsåbning i New York
Trump's rescue of Nvidia's Huang brings political risks

segments.body: Nvidia shares fell about 8% after trading opened in New York on Wednesday, while the Nasdaq dropped more than 4% and the S&P 500 fell 3%. The move followed a 31% one-day rise after Huang returned to the company, according to investment strategist Jacob Pedersen, who described the earlier jump as driven more by emotion than company figures.

segments.title: Political stakes
segments.body: The market reversal comes amid scrutiny of Trump’s public intervention in Huang’s return and lawmakers’ plans to examine Nvidia’s China-linked chip business. The BBC reports that the president has said officials cleared Huang, while members of Congress have promised oversight; the consequences for the company and its political ties remain unresolved.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s analysis argues Trump has tied his political fortunes to Nvidia’s success and warns that questions about AI, export controls and the president’s intervention could keep the company under a harsher spotlight.

content.headline: China investigates Shanghai party chief in widening anti-corruption purge
content.shortHeadline: China probes Shanghai chief in widening party purge
content.standfirst: Chen Jining, a member of the Communist Party’s elite Politburo, is being investigated over alleged disciplinary and legal violations. It is the fourth current Politburo member to face a probe, an unusually broad purge ahead of next year’s leadership appointments.

image.caption: Chen Jining, the Shanghai party chief under investigation in China’s anti-corruption drive.

sources.originalTitle: Xi's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star in Chinese Communist Party

segments.body: Chinese authorities are investigating Chen Jining, the 62-year-old party chief of Shanghai, for suspected “severe violations of discipline and laws”, according to the party’s anti-corruption body. He has not been removed from the Politburo, but the BBC says officials rarely return after such investigations.

segments.title: Uncertainty at the top
segments.body: The investigation makes Chen the fourth member of the Politburo appointed in 2022 to face a probe, in the broadest purge of the body in several decades. The move comes as the party prepares to appoint new leaders next year; analysts say the investigation adds uncertainty about who may feel secure in the current leadership.

content.headline: Ukraine says it damaged five Russian jets in airfield strike
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine claims five Russian jets hit in airfield strike
content.standfirst: Kyiv says three MiG-31s and two Su-34s were hit at Savasleyka, an airfield used by aircraft that launch missiles and glide bombs at Ukraine. Russia has not commented, and the extent of the damage remains unclear.

image.caption: A Russian MiG-31, one of the aircraft Ukraine says it hit at Savasleyka airfield.

sources.originalTitle: Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine

segments.body: Ukraine’s General Staff says an attack damaged five Russian aircraft at Savasleyka airfield, about 300km east of Moscow. The airfield hosts aircraft used to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs against Ukraine. Kyiv says it is still assessing the damage; Russia has not commented on the reported strike.

segments.title: Other reported strikes
segments.body: Kyiv also says it hit two oil refineries in Russia’s Samara region, as well as radar, fuel and logistics sites in occupied Ukrainian territory. The governor of Samara region reported that one person was killed and power outages affected several towns during overnight attacks.

content.headline: Colombian forces free hostages after 17-hour supermarket siege
content.shortHeadline: Colombian forces free hostages after 17-hour siege
content.standfirst: Police and special forces rescued around 20 shoppers and employees from a supermarket in Cartagena. One gunman was killed and four were arrested; authorities say the siege followed an attempted robbery of an armoured cash vehicle.

image.caption: Relatives wait anxiously as the hostage situation unfolds in Cartagena.

sources.originalTitle: Colombian police storm supermarket to free 20 held hostage for 17 hours

segments.body: Colombian security forces freed around 20 shoppers and employees after a 17-hour hostage ordeal at a Cartagena supermarket. One gunman was killed during the operation and four people were arrested, according to police. The hostages were being checked by medical teams and reunited with their families.

segments.title: How the siege unfolded
segments.body: The gunmen entered the supermarket after an attempted robbery of an armoured vehicle carrying cash, President Abelardo de la Espriella said. They had earlier released 10 people but continued to hold others while seeking a getaway. Authorities say the assailants had no political affiliation.

content.headline: Hera mission prepares close-up images of asteroid hit in Earth-defence test
content.shortHeadline: Hera prepares close-ups of asteroid struck in defence test
content.standfirst: The European Space Agency spacecraft is examining Dimorphos, which NASA deliberately struck in 2022. Its measurements will help scientists understand how an impact changes an asteroid’s orbit and what might be needed to deflect a future threat.

image.caption: The Hera spacecraft is studying Dimorphos, the asteroid struck in NASA’s 2022 test.

sources.originalTitle: Close-up images to be revealed of asteroid deliberately hit to test ability to protect Earth

segments.body: The European Space Agency’s Hera mission is studying Dimorphos, the smaller member of a pair of asteroids that NASA’s DART spacecraft deliberately hit in 2022. Images of the impact’s aftermath are due to be released on Wednesday; Hera will investigate whether the collision left a crater or reshaped the asteroid.

segments.title: Learning from the impact
segments.body: DART shortened Dimorphos’s orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes, showing that a spacecraft can alter an asteroid’s path. Hera will measure the asteroid’s mass and study the impact site, helping scientists estimate what size and speed of spacecraft might be needed to deflect a future object on a collision course with Earth.

content.headline: Poundland enters administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk
content.shortHeadline: Poundland enters administration as 12,000 jobs are at risk
content.standfirst: The discount retailer will keep trading while administrators seek a buyer for its 600 stores and distribution centres. Its US owner rejected last-ditch bids, leaving a breakup and substantial job losses as possible outcomes.

image.caption: A Poundland store in the UK as the retailer enters administration.

sources.originalTitle: Poundland collapses into administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk

segments.body: Poundland’s directors have appointed administrators, putting about 12,000 jobs at risk across the retailer’s 600 stores in the UK and Ireland. The chain will continue trading while administrators explore a sale of the business or its assets, in whole or in part.

segments.title: Rescue bids rejected
segments.body: Poundland’s US owner, Gordon Brothers, said a sales process had found no viable way to save the company as a whole. It rejected at least two last-minute bids, and administrators say the chain was running short of funds to restock for the Christmas trading period.

content.headline: Ministers accept fast-track route and fewer reviews in proposed PIP overhaul
content.shortHeadline: PIP review: fast-track claims accepted, wider reforms undecided
content.standfirst: Ministers have accepted proposals to fast-track some severe and end-of-life claims and reduce repeat reviews for people with lasting conditions. The wider plan to assess extra costs could change payments, but details and effects remain uncertain.

image.caption: A protester takes part in a rally against disability benefit cuts.

sources.originalTitle: The benefit claimants who will be shielded from PIP cuts
All PIP changes announced – from fast-track routes to ending unnecessary reviews
All the people who could lose PIP cash under new reforms
I was a PIP assessor – this is how the system sets people up to fail

segments.body: The government has accepted two recommendations from the review of Personal Independence Payments: a fast-track route for some people with severe, well-evidenced conditions and those nearing the end of life, and fewer repeat assessments for people with lifelong or progressive conditions. Ministers have not yet said when the changes will begin or set out final eligibility criteria.

segments.title: The wider assessment is unsettled
segments.body: The review also proposes replacing the current points-based test with an assessment of people’s needs and disability-related costs. Ministers have not accepted that recommendation, and it remains unclear whether some claimants would receive less. The proposals for under-25s are also unresolved: Alan Milburn’s review suggests a separate allowance, while the Timms review recommends keeping PIP for all ages.

perspectives.body: A former PIP assessor warns that costs can be difficult to document and may not reflect someone’s actual needs, raising concern that a new assessment could leave some disabled people with less support.

content.headline: Energy price cap to lift typical annual bill by 26% in January
content.shortHeadline: January energy cap to push typical annual bill up 26%
content.standfirst: Ofgem says a typical household on a variable tariff will pay the equivalent of £2,166 a year from January, up £443. The cap applies to unit rates rather than total bills, so actual costs depend on energy use and tariff.

image.caption: Ofgem’s new energy price cap takes effect in January.

sources.originalTitle: How much your energy bills will jump in January – by the size of your home

segments.body: Ofgem’s new price cap means a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay the equivalent of £2,166 a year from January, up from £1,723. The increase is about 26%, or £443 annually, for customers on variable tariffs paying by direct debit.

segments.title: Who will feel the rise
segments.body: The cap limits the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can set; it does not cap a household’s total bill. Around 20 million households on standard variable tariffs will be affected. Fixed-tariff customers will not see the increase until their deal ends, while households that use more energy will pay more.

content.headline: Burnham launches inquiry into records of nuclear test veterans
content.shortHeadline: Inquiry to examine records of UK nuclear test veterans
content.standfirst: An independent panel will investigate blood tests conducted on service personnel during Britain’s nuclear weapons trials. Around 22,000 military personnel took part in 45 tests between 1952 and 1967, and many veterans have long sought access to the records.

image.caption: Veterans and supporters meet Andy Burnham as campaigners seek answers about nuclear test records.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham launches inquiry into nuclear bomb test veterans’ records

segments.body: Andy Burnham has launched an independent inquiry into a programme of blood tests on service personnel exposed to nuclear weapons trials. Former bishop of Liverpool James Jones, who chaired the Hillsborough panel, will lead the investigation, which aims to produce an interim report in time for the 75th anniversary of the first UK nuclear test.

segments.title: Decades-long campaign
segments.body: About 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale tests in Australia and the South Pacific from 1952 to 1967. Veterans have campaigned for decades for access to records they believe may help establish links between exposure and illnesses. The Ministry of Defence has admitted conducting biological examinations after previously denying them to Parliament and the courts.

content.headline: UK secretly resettled refugee in Eswatini, where he later died
content.shortHeadline: UK sent refugee to Eswatini under undisclosed deal
content.standfirst: A Sri Lankan refugee with a history of severe mental illness was transferred to Eswatini under a draft deal that was not disclosed to Parliament or the local community. He died by suicide months later; questions remain about safeguards and the agreement’s oversight.

image.caption: Mbabane, the capital of Eswatini, where the UK resettled a refugee under a draft agreement.

sources.originalTitle: UK sent sex offender refugee to African country in undisclosed deal

segments.body: The UK forcibly resettled Kishanth Peramalya, a Sri Lankan refugee and convicted sex offender, in Eswatini, a country with which he had no connection. A draft agreement seen by the BBC shows the UK would cover accommodation, healthcare and other support for up to three years. Peramalya died by suicide months after arriving there.

segments.title: Questions over safeguards
segments.body: Peramalya had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts. His family told the BBC he was initially placed alone in a guesthouse and that his mental health worsened. The deal was not disclosed to Parliament or the local community; the document does not state a total cost or explain how the two governments would manage risks. The UK says protecting the public is its priority.

content.headline: Labour stands by conversion practices bill amid dispute over its scope
content.shortHeadline: Labour backs conversion practices bill despite calls to change it
content.standfirst: The government says it remains committed to a bill banning abusive attempts to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity. Supporters say survivors need protection, while critics warn that the draft could affect family, religious and healthcare conversations.

image.caption: Shash Appan, who says she experienced years of abuse over her sexuality and gender identity.

sources.originalTitle: Labour ‘committed’ to ban on conversion practices despite calls for proposed law to be scrapped
‘They wanted me to conform’: people abused over sexuality and gender identity tell their stories

segments.body: Equalities minister Bridget Phillipson says Labour remains committed to banning conversion practices in England and Wales. The draft bill would make abusive attempts to change someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity punishable by an unlimited fine and up to five years in prison, and would allow courts to issue protection orders before serious harm occurs.

segments.title: Support and concern
segments.body: Survivors and LGBTQ+ groups say abusive practices continue and the law should protect people at risk. Critics, including religious leaders and former review chair Hilary Cass, argue the draft needs changes to avoid chilling appropriate parenting, pastoral care or healthcare conversations. The bill is still under scrutiny, and its final scope is not settled.

perspectives.body: Survivor Shash Appan supports the bill’s broad aim but says it focuses too heavily on punishment and too little on prevention and practical help for people trying to escape abuse.

content.headline: UK survey finds a third of young adults have never had sex
content.shortHeadline: A third of young Britons aged 16–24 have never had sex
content.standfirst: A new national survey finds that more young people have never had sex than in earlier studies, while many report sexting and watching pornography. Researchers say the study shows changing patterns but cannot explain what is driving them.

sources.originalTitle: Third of young Brits have never had sex, but many are sexting and watching porn

segments.body: A third of people aged 16 to 24 have never had sex, up from about one in five in earlier surveys, according to the latest National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles. Half of this age group said they had sent or received sexual images in the past year, and many also reported watching pornography.

segments.title: What the survey can—and cannot—show
segments.body: Among adults under 45, the average reported frequency of sex has fallen from about once a week in 1990 to twice a month. Researchers say factors such as drinking less, living with parents, mental health and the effects of the pandemic may play a part, but the survey does not establish a cause.

content.headline: Public prosecutors in Denmark to be barred from wearing religious headscarves in
content.shortHeadline: Denmark to bar prosecutors from wearing religious headscarves in court
content.standfirst: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked the Director of Public Prosecutions to introduce new rules requiring state prosecutors to appear religiously and politically neutral in court. Prosecutor Zahra Sediqi says the change limits women’s choices.

image.caption: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked for new guidelines on religious dress for prosecutors in court.

sources.originalTitle: Minister strammer reglerne: Offentlige anklagere må ikke bære religiøse tørklæder
Her er Zahra. Hun kan ikke længere være anklager i retten

segments.body: Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen has asked the Director of Public Prosecutions to issue internal guidelines barring religious headscarves for public prosecutors representing the state in criminal cases. The rules are due to take effect “as soon as possible”; judges already face a comparable restriction under law.

segments.title: The prosecutor’s objection
segments.body: Zahra Sediqi, a prosecutor who wears a headscarf, says the change limits women’s opportunities on the basis of religion and does not make a person neutral. Wammen says the rules are intended to ensure that state prosecutors appear impartial in court.

perspectives.body: Sediqi says a courtroom robe and professional role define her work as a prosecutor, and argues that removing a headscarf cannot by itself make someone impartial.

content.headline: Rockwool shares fall more than 15% after earnings miss and lower outlook
content.shortHeadline: Rockwool shares tumble more than 15% after outlook cut
content.standfirst: The Danish insulation company’s shares fell sharply after a disappointing third quarter and a lower forecast for 2026. Chief executive Jes Munk Hansen blamed faster-than-expected energy price rises that the company could not match with price increases.

sources.originalTitle: Rockwool får kursklø efter skuffende regnskab - aktien falder over 15 procent

segments.body: Rockwool shares fell by more than 15% after the Danish insulation group reported a disappointing third quarter and cut its expectations for 2026. Chief executive Jes Munk Hansen said energy prices rose faster than the company could adjust its own prices.
Munk Hansen said the rapid shifts in energy costs made it difficult to decide when to raise or lower prices. Rockwool has already increased prices by 5% this year, he told MarketWire.

content.headline: Five teenagers injured in serious crash near Borup; municipality offers support
content.shortHeadline: Five teenagers injured in Borup crash; school offered crisis help
content.standfirst: A car carrying five teenagers aged 15 and 16 hit a tree near Borup. Two were in critical condition and three were stable, police told DR; Køge Municipality is offering psychological support to affected pupils and teachers.

sources.originalTitle: Kommune tilbyder krisehjælp efter alvorlig trafikulykke med mindreårige

segments.body: Five teenagers, aged 15 and 16, were injured when a car struck a tree near Borup on Tuesday. Two were taken to Rigshospitalet in critical condition; the other three were reported stable at hospitals in Copenhagen and Køge. Police told DR on Wednesday afternoon that the teenagers’ conditions were unchanged.

segments.title: Support at school
segments.body: Køge Municipality is offering psychological help to pupils in the affected class and their teachers at a school in Borup. Mayor Ken Kristensen said the support would remain available for as long as needed.

content.headline: Archaeologists search beneath Ribe Cathedral for early churches and royal graves
content.shortHeadline: Archaeologists dig beneath Ribe Cathedral for early church remains
content.standfirst: Excavations during a DKK 170m restoration could uncover remains of earlier churches, including the wooden church associated with Ansgar. The cathedral’s main room is due to close from mid-May until Easter 2029.

image.caption: The first limestone floor tiles have been removed in Ribe Cathedral ahead of archaeological excavations.

sources.originalTitle: Domkirke skal lukkes i to år, mens der graves efter gamle konger og kirker

segments.body: Archaeologists have begun examining the ground beneath Ribe Cathedral as part of a major restoration. They are looking for traces of earlier buildings, including the wooden church associated with Ansgar, dating to the ninth century, and for the grave of King Erik Emune, who died in 1137.

segments.title: A long restoration
segments.body: The restoration, budgeted at about DKK 170m, will include underfloor heating to address damp that threatens historic objects. Areas of the cathedral are already partly closed; the main church space is expected to close from mid-May next year until Easter 2029 while work continues.

content.headline: Bisca recalls æbleskiver and biscuits after grain contamination case
content.shortHeadline: Bisca recalls æbleskiver and biscuits over contaminated grain
content.standfirst: The food company says the products were made with flour from grain stored at a site where inspectors found rodent droppings, dead mice and mould. The recall includes some products with best-before dates in 2027 and others whose dates have passed.

sources.originalTitle: Æbleskiver og kiks tilbagekaldes i sag om korn-lager med rottelort

segments.body: Bisca is recalling æbleskiver and biscuits made with flour supplied by Valsemøllen, after a food-safety case involving grain stored at a Zealand site. Inspectors found rodent droppings, dead mice and mould there, according to DR’s report.

The recall covers products with best-before dates in 2027 as well as some with dates that have already passed and may still be in consumers’ cupboards. Bisca has published a list of affected products.

content.headline: Danish couple decide together to remain child-free after years of uncertainty
content.shortHeadline: Danish couple choose a life without children together
content.standfirst: Bianca and Nicolaj began considering a breakup when they realised they wanted different futures. After time to reflect, Nicolaj says he also wants a life without children; the couple have bought a home near Aarhus and plan to travel.

sources.originalTitle: For et år siden tog Nicolajs kæreste en beslutning. Hun vil ikke have børn. Og så måtte han overveje sin egen fremtid

segments.body: Bianca Van Urk had long said she did not want children, while Nicolaj Hesberg expected he might become a father. Their disagreement became a serious strain on their relationship, and in a television programme he said that if he chose to have children, they would have to separate.

segments.title: A decision together
segments.body: Seven months after filming ended, Hesberg told DR he had decided he also wanted a life without children. The couple say they feel calmer about their future, have bought a house in Lystrup near Aarhus and plan to focus on friends and travel. They say they remain open to change.

content.headline: Beatles’ Savile Row rooftop site approved as visitor attraction
content.shortHeadline: Beatles’ Savile Row site approved, but no rooftop gigs
content.standfirst: A seven-storey exhibition and cultural attraction is planned for the building where the Beatles were based and played their final public show. The approval comes with a ban on live music on the rooftop.

image.caption: The Beatles performing on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row in 1969.

sources.originalTitle: Beatles attraction at 3 Savile Row approved – with ban on rooftop gigs

segments.body: Westminster council has unanimously approved plans to turn 3 Savile Row, the Beatles’ former headquarters and the site of their 1969 rooftop performance, into a seven-storey exhibition and cultural attraction. Apple Corps has said it hopes to open the venue in 2027.

segments.title: A rooftop without live music
segments.body: Visitors will be able to access the roof, but live music is prohibited. Amplified music will be allowed at controlled noise levels. The plans also include a cafe-bar, a replica studio and an exhibition shop; a booking system is intended to prevent queues.

The Savile Row Bespoke Association raised concerns about congestion on the street’s narrow pavements and the effect of visitor numbers on local businesses. Apple Corps estimates the attraction could draw up to 900 people a day on weekdays and 1,140 at weekends.

content.headline: Peter Gabriel on a new album, AI and the ideas that keep derailing him
content.shortHeadline: Peter Gabriel on AI, music and the joy of getting sidetracked
content.standfirst: The musician’s 13-track, 90-minute album arrives with two mixes, but an interview ranges from creativity and artificial intelligence to consciousness and animal communication. His digressions, he says, feed the work.

image.caption: Peter Gabriel, whose interests range from music to artificial intelligence and animal communication.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel

segments.body: Peter Gabriel’s new album, o\i, runs nearly 90 minutes and will be released in two versions: a “dark” mix by Tchad Blake and a “bright” one by Mark “Spike” Stent. Gabriel describes the long songs as an extension of his interest in African music and his willingness, at 76, to make what he wants.

segments.title: A creative mind in motion
segments.body: An interview about the record wanders through Gabriel’s interests in consciousness, communication with other species and scientific research. He sees his diversions as part of his creative process: conversations and ideas outside the album cycle, he argues, can enrich the music.

segments.title: Tools and risks
segments.body: Gabriel is enthusiastic about AI as a creative tool, but says its use in warfare is frightening and calls for international agreements, safeguards and a means of control. He also speculates about people becoming more closely integrated with AI; these are his views, not settled predictions.

content.headline: Life Without Buildings reunite after their music finds a new audience
content.shortHeadline: Life Without Buildings return after a TikTok-fuelled rediscovery
content.standfirst: The Glasgow band split in 2002 after a brief, obscure run. A Frank Ocean play and a viral TikTok helped new listeners find their idiosyncratic music, but the returning group worried that reunion gigs might diminish what they had left behind.

image.caption: Life Without Buildings pictured around the release of their debut album.

sources.originalTitle: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?

segments.body: Life Without Buildings played their first proper gig together in almost 25 years at Glasgow’s Mono. The band, whose brief career produced one album, Any Other City, and a handful of singles, are back for four shows linked to Rough Trade’s 50th-anniversary celebrations.

segments.title: An unexpected second life
segments.body: The group’s rediscovery gathered pace after Frank Ocean played “The Leanover” on his Apple Music show in 2018. Later, a TikTok video of Beabadoobee miming to the song’s opening seconds helped it travel further. Singer Sue Tompkins’ spoken, rhythmic vocals remain central to the band’s singular sound.

The musicians say they had been wary of returning, concerned that new attention might spoil their memory of a joyful but commercially difficult time. Their first reunion performance brought the old songs back to life, Tompkins said, and left her energised by playing with her bandmates again.

content.headline: Judee Sill’s music finds new listeners decades after her death
content.shortHeadline: Judee Sill’s overlooked songs are finding new listeners
content.standfirst: The singer-songwriter’s intricate folk and gospel music once drew critical acclaim, but her career faded and she died aged 35. Covers by later artists and a documentary are bringing renewed attention to a catalogue that still feels precarious.

image.caption: Judee Sill in London in 1972, as her music career was beginning to rise.

sources.originalTitle: The forgotten folk genius who’s finally getting her due after dying in obscurity

segments.body: Judee Sill’s two albums combined folk, country and gospel with complex arrangements and devotional songwriting. Signed to David Geffen’s Asylum Records, she was once presented as a rising star, but her second album, Heart Food, did not sell well and she was dropped from the label.

segments.title: A difficult life, a lasting body of work
segments.body: Sill faced addiction, homelessness, prison, violence and chronic pain. She died in 1979 at 35. The account notes uncertainty about the circumstances of her death: it was ruled a suicide, although some believe the note found nearby was a plea for help rather than a suicide note.

Her songs have been covered by artists including Fleet Foxes, Weyes Blood and Big Thief. The documentary Lost Angel and the release of her final recordings have also helped introduce her work to new listeners, though the piece argues that her place in the wider musical canon remains fragile.

content.headline: Weird Baile’s internet-born Brazilian funk gets an archival release
content.shortHeadline: Weird Baile’s lost Brazilian funk finds an official release
content.standfirst: TraTraTrax has assembled tracks made over two decades by an online collective working on the fringes of Brazilian funk. The review hears an influential, carefully sequenced archive, though its dark minimalism leaves some of the group’s playful side behind.

sources.originalTitle: Collected Rips 2004-2024

segments.body: Collected Rips 2004-2024 brings together 14 previously unreleased tracks by Weird Baile, an internet-based group of Brazilian producers and DJs. The label says the recordings were assembled from MP3 rips, voice notes and lost project files, preserving music that helped shape an online strand of funk.

segments.title: A scene without a single home
segments.body: The review describes the collective as rooted in the internet rather than a particular city or baile. Its tracks draw on different regional forms of Brazilian funk and outside references, from Migos samples to UK bass, creating a sound shaped by online circulation as much as by local scenes.

The compilation’s dark, sparse beats make for a coherent listen, and the closing track brings a more playful, loose energy. The reviewer’s reservation is that the selection could have included more of the fun that made Weird Baile intriguing in the first place.

content.headline: Thoom fuses Arabic instrumentation and hyperpop on a vivid debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom turns hyperpop into a vivid, personal debut
content.standfirst: The Beirut-raised, Los Angeles-based artist brings oud and other Arabic sounds into abrasive club pop, making space for both theatrical excess and vulnerable songwriting. The record’s closing song turns toward Lebanon and the uncertainty of return.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, Thoom—artist Zeynab Marwan—joins hyperpop production with Arabic instrumentation. The review describes a sound that moves between pounding club tracks, pop drama and quieter, more ominous songs, with Marwan’s voice able to shift from melodic warmth to menace.

segments.title: Intensity with feeling
segments.body: The review hears the strongest work in songs where volatile production deepens the emotional material rather than overwhelming it. “Morocco” turns a lover’s cruelty into a restrained threat, while the fierce “On the Floor” puts Marwan’s voice against relentless drums and sharp synths.

Closer “I’m Going Back to Lebanon” links longing for home with uncertainty about the country’s future. The reviewer calls it the clearest expression of the album’s stakes, while finding some of the more conventional pop moments less distinctive.

content.headline: Armand Hammer’s new album turns everyday scenes into political writing
content.shortHeadline: Armand Hammer turn daily life into urgent political rap
content.standfirst: On Snakes & Ladders, billy woods and Elucid bring together a wide circle of independent producers for fractured, searching rap. The review hears a record that connects personal observation with the pressures of race, power and political anxiety.

sources.originalTitle: Snakes & Ladders

segments.body: Snakes & Ladders, surprise-released by Backwoodz Studioz, is a new album from New York duo Armand Hammer. Across dense, fragmented verses, billy woods and Elucid draw meaning from ordinary settings—a street walk, a job application—and connect those moments to broader histories of power and displacement.

segments.title: A collective sound
segments.body: The production comes from a broad roster of collaborators, including clipping., Preservation, Kenny Segal and Child Actor. Despite the range of contributors, the review finds a shared atmosphere: unsettling, varied beats that give the rappers room to move between sharply different writing and vocal styles.

The review frames the album’s political weight as an alternative measure of rap’s cultural value, beyond commercial success. It describes the record as demanding rather than easy listening, with its anxieties and histories deliberately left unresolved.

content.headline: Font’s American Bully XL brings country ache into industrial noise
content.shortHeadline: Font bring country heartbreak into noisy, confessional songs
content.standfirst: The Texas band’s second album trades some of its debut’s obscurity for more exposed songwriting. Its warped country references and abrasive production make the vulnerability feel less like a change of style than a new source of tension.

sources.originalTitle: American Bully XL

segments.body: On American Bully XL, Font move toward more direct, confessional lyrics while keeping the industrial distortion and restless arrangements of their earlier work. The review hears songs about heartbreak and the desire for recognition, delivered through a crowded mix of synths, sampling, guitars and percussion.

segments.title: Tenderness through distortion
segments.body: The album’s country influence appears in fragments: fingerpicking, wavering keyboard lines and ballad-like melodies, often blurred by harsh production. On “Texas,” the sounds shift between something like lap steel and a dial tone as the narrator pleads for a relationship to return.

content.headline: 14th review: Ava DuVernay makes a forceful case for the US Constitution
content.shortHeadline: Ava DuVernay’s 14th defends constitutional rights
content.standfirst: In her follow-up to 13th, DuVernay turns to the 14th Amendment and the rights it established. The review praises the documentary’s historical argument and its urgent defence of those protections against contemporary threats.

image.caption: Ava DuVernay in her documentary 14th.

sources.originalTitle: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants

segments.body: Ava DuVernay’s 14th examines the constitutional amendment that established birthright citizenship, due process and equal protection under the law. The film also considers the amendment’s bar on insurrectionists holding public office, arguing that these provisions are under threat.

segments.title: History and the present
segments.body: The review highlights the film’s account of the Reconstruction amendments after the American Civil War, and the backlash that followed. DuVernay draws a parallel between that history and what the reviewer describes as a contemporary reaction to Barack Obama’s presidency.

content.headline: Why Hollywood keeps returning to its imagined golden age
content.shortHeadline: Hollywood’s nostalgia boom meets an industry in crisis
content.standfirst: A new Cliff Booth film joins a wave of stories looking back at old Los Angeles. The feature argues that the appeal of that Hollywood past is inseparable from the present-day film industry’s job losses, shrinking production and fears about AI.

image.caption: Quentin Tarantino with Leonardo DiCaprio and Brad Pitt during the making of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.

sources.originalTitle: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories

segments.body: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is part of a recent run of films revisiting Los Angeles and Hollywood’s past, alongside works by Paul Thomas Anderson, Damien Chazelle and Ti West. These films look back to the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s through the stories and atmosphere of an earlier city.

segments.title: Nostalgia in a changing industry
segments.body: The feature links this revival to a present marked by declining local production, post-pandemic box-office pressures and significant job losses. It also notes the anxiety that AI could further hollow out film work and the city’s creative infrastructure.

The piece questions whether the films are recovering an authentic golden age or reproducing Hollywood’s longstanding talent for fabrication. It points to Los Angeles Plays Itself as a more sceptical account of a city built on constant reinvention.

content.headline: Jane Alexander looks back on five decades of acting and arts advocacy
content.shortHeadline: Jane Alexander on a career shaped by theatre and public service
content.standfirst: The actor recalls her breakthrough in The Great White Hope, a career spanning film and theatre, and her time leading the US National Endowment for the Arts. She also discusses harassment in the industry and the struggle to keep public arts funding available.

image.caption: Jane Alexander, who says she is glad the #MeToo movement brought harassment into the open.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom

segments.body: Jane Alexander’s performance in The Great White Hope brought her a Tony Award, a husband and her first film role. The play, about boxer Jack Johnson and an interracial marriage in segregated America, also brought her hate mail and death threats. Alexander remembers Muhammad Ali seeing his own story in the production.

segments.title: Work, power and the arts
segments.body: Alexander says the casting couch was an overt part of the industry: she turned down advances, while recognising that other actresses faced different choices and vulnerabilities. She welcomes the #MeToo movement. Later, as chair of the National Endowment for the Arts, she travelled widely to argue that access to art should extend beyond major cities.

She warns that cuts to arts funding threaten access for audiences and support for complex work, while noting that theatre prices already limit who can attend. At 87, Alexander says she has no plans to retire and remains committed to both art and nature.

content.headline: Josephine turns a director’s childhood trauma into a difficult film
content.shortHeadline: Josephine asks what a child carries after witnessing rape
content.standfirst: Beth de Araújo’s drama draws on an assault she witnessed as a child and follows an eight-year-old struggling to understand what she saw. The film’s graphic opening and its approach to young performers raise difficult questions about depicting sexual violence.

image.caption: Beth de Araújo with Channing Tatum, Mason Reeves and Gemma Chan.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine

segments.body: Writer-director Beth de Araújo says she drew on her own childhood experience for Josephine. In the film, an eight-year-old witnesses a rape and begins to interpret the world around her through fear. The story follows her confusion and her parents’ attempts to help, which do not immediately address what she needs to know.

segments.title: A deliberate choice
segments.body: The film shows the assault Josephine witnesses in graphic detail. De Araújo argues that the audience needs to see what the child sees to understand the fear shaping the rest of the story. The child actor, Mason Reeves, was not present for the assault scene and did not read the script.

The feature also describes how the film draws on de Araújo’s work as a witness advocate and on research into sexual-assault cases. She says she does not regard trauma as something that is simply resolved, and that the film’s release has nevertheless coincided with her being able to sleep through the night.

content.headline: Way of the Warrior Kid review: Chris Pratt’s film turns bullying into boot camp
content.shortHeadline: Way of the Warrior Kid treats bullying with military drills
content.standfirst: The review faults this family film for answering a bullied boy’s problems with physical training and cage-fighting. It argues that the story’s easy celebration of machismo misses the chance to treat its young characters and their family circumstances with more care.

image.caption: Chris Pratt and Jude Hill in Way of the Warrior Kid.

sources.originalTitle: Way of the Warrior Kid review - Chris Pratt’s family film is as subtle as a military recruitment video

segments.body: In Way of the Warrior Kid, a bullied 13-year-old is put through a strict training plan by his Navy SEAL uncle. The routine includes exercise, chores and a summer job, but also cage-fighting—an escalation the review sees as an implausible response to the boy’s troubles.

segments.title: A missed opportunity
segments.body: The reviewer finds the film’s treatment of the boy’s widowed mother especially ungenerous, and says any suggestions that the uncle is carrying trauma from combat are quickly brushed aside. The third act offers some excitement, but does not undo the film’s broader reliance on machismo and military imagery.

content.headline: The Slightest Touch follows Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s friendship
content.shortHeadline: Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s friendship on screen
content.standfirst: Rachel Fleit’s documentary follows Farrell and Fogarty as they prepare for the Dublin Marathon, with Farrell set to push her wheelchair for the final miles. The review finds a warm friendship story that also allows space for Farrell’s grief and family life.

image.caption: Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty in The Slightest Touch.

sources.originalTitle: The Slightest Touch review – running marathons in Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s odd-couple friendship

segments.body: Emma Fogarty, an advocate for people with epidermolysis bullosa, has a long friendship with Colin Farrell, who supports the Irish charity Debra. The documentary follows them preparing for the 2025 Dublin Marathon, where Farrell runs and pushes Fogarty in her modified wheelchair for the final two miles.

segments.title: More than a race
segments.body: The film also shows Farrell speaking about his father’s final weeks and his eldest son, who has Angelman syndrome. The reviewer describes him as emotionally open while noting that the documentary keeps much of the pair’s private lives carefully controlled.

content.headline: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth brings Brad Pitt back to 1977 LA
content.shortHeadline: Brad Pitt returns as Cliff Booth in a 1970s LA caper
content.standfirst: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s continuation of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, with Pitt’s stuntman turned fixer at its centre. The review enjoys the film’s energy and comic style while noting that it leaves key questions and much of its story unresolved.

image.caption: Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

sources.originalTitle: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return

segments.body: Set in Los Angeles in 1977, the film follows Cliff Booth after he has left stunt work and taken on a collection of side jobs, including discreetly helping people in the film industry who are being extorted. Elizabeth Debicki’s talent agent brings him into a new criminal entanglement.

segments.title: Pitt’s easygoing centre
segments.body: The review praises Brad Pitt’s imperturbable performance, which gives the film its comic charge, and describes Fincher’s direction as brisker than Tarantino’s chapter-driven style. It also notes how the film leaves the question of Cliff’s wife largely untouched.

content.headline: You Can See Everything blurs Nathan Fielder’s documentary and its subject
content.shortHeadline: A documentary turns Elizabeth Holmes into an uneasy puzzle
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder’s film follows Elizabeth Holmes and her family before her prison sentence, raising questions about truth, sympathy and control over a public image. The review is captivated by the experiment but uneasy about how its subject’s story is reframed.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.

sources.originalTitle: Elizabeth Holmes is not the villain of You Can See Everything. That’s a problem

segments.body: You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes in the month before she reports to prison for her Theranos fraud conviction. Holmes and her husband invited a film crew into their home, seeking to tell a more personal story after years of public scrutiny.

segments.title: Who controls the story?
segments.body: Director Nathan Fielder is known for work that blurs documentary and performance. The review describes him watching Holmes closely while questioning whether she is sincere, manipulative or both—an uncertainty that grows as he becomes more involved in her life.

The review finds the film’s second half changes focus toward Holmes’s husband, whose behaviour and use of an AI model of her complicate the story further. It argues that this shift risks making Holmes seem more sympathetic, while leaving unresolved how much of what the audience sees is performance.

content.headline: Blade Runner 2099 review: a neon-lit vision of a world turned upside down
content.shortHeadline: Blade Runner 2099 is a haunting TV expansion of the films
content.standfirst: Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer lead the franchise’s first television story, set decades after Blade Runner 2049. The review praises its haunting visual world and mood, while wishing it made more room for episodic storytelling.

image.caption: A neon-lit scene from Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099 review – every scene of this TV version is packed with terrifying visual beauty

segments.body: In Blade Runner 2099, replicants have become blade runners, hunting disobedient humans. Michelle Yeoh plays Olwen, an ageing replicant, and Hunter Schafer plays Cora, a human impersonating one. Their search for a former colleague becomes a story about memory and identity.

segments.title: Atmosphere over explanation
segments.body: The review values the series’ images and mood over a fully explained world: neon, shadow, abandoned spaces and a soundtrack of synths and saxophone. It also finds sharp visual unease in details such as the devices used to restrain people and the places where replicants imitate human life.

The series brings the franchise’s questions about memory into an era of anxiety about machine-made images and text. The reviewer finds its doomsday visions memorable, though argues that a clearer episodic structure might have strengthened the story.

content.headline: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure finds joy in friendship and memory
content.shortHeadline: Prue and Sandi’s South African trip is a joyful travelogue
content.standfirst: Prue Leith revisits places she knew growing up in South Africa, accompanied by Sandi Toksvig. The review celebrates their easy friendship while also highlighting Leith’s reflections on apartheid and the country’s changing present.

image.caption: Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig in Simon’s Town, South Africa.

sources.originalTitle: Prue and Sandi’s South African Adventure review – you’ll feel lucky to have this joyful show in your life

segments.body: The six-part series follows Prue Leith and Sandi Toksvig around South Africa. Leith, who left the country for England at 20, revisits places from her childhood, while Toksvig’s lively curiosity turns the trip into an affectionate two-hander.

segments.title: Memory and history
segments.body: In Cape Town, Leith remembers the city of her youth and speaks with a woman whose family was forcibly moved during apartheid. Leith says she was raised to oppose apartheid but feels ashamed that she was not more conscious of everyday injustices as a teenager.

The review finds the series’ warmth in the pair’s friendship and their willingness to reflect as well as enjoy the journey. Leith says she wanted to make the programme while she and Toksvig were still able to travel together.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson gives The Great British Bake Off a fresh flavour
content.shortHeadline: Nigella Lawson brings new energy to Bake Off
content.standfirst: The review credits Lawson’s vivid food commentary, warmth and camp humour with helping revive the baking competition. It also points to strong viewing figures and format changes as signs that the show’s latest series has connected with audiences.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson with fellow Bake Off judge Paul Hollywood.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The icing on the cake’: how Nigella saved Bake Off

segments.body: Nigella Lawson has replaced Prue Leith as a judge on The Great British Bake Off, alongside Paul Hollywood. The review says Lawson’s enthusiastic attention to flavour and gift for description have made her a distinctive presence in the tent.

segments.title: A change in the mix
segments.body: The programme has added new formats, including an Audience Choice week and challenges based on illustrations rather than recipes. The article reports that the first episode drew 7.1 million viewers, ahead of Strictly Come Dancing’s launch episode, and says Channel 4 has signed Lawson for another series.

content.headline: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle makes history a lively tour
content.shortHeadline: Lucy Worsley unlocks the history behind Europe’s castles
content.standfirst: Worsley’s four-part series explores the Doge’s Palace, Versailles, Blenheim and Neuschwanstein. The review praises her accessible approach and the programme’s ability to connect grand buildings with the power, politics and people behind them.

image.caption: Lucy Worsley exploring Venice’s Doge’s Palace.

sources.originalTitle: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle review – heavenly TV that instantly brightens up your day

segments.body: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle begins at Venice’s Doge’s Palace and continues to Versailles, Blenheim and Neuschwanstein. The review praises Worsley for inviting other historians into the story and making complex history easy to follow.

segments.title: The stories inside the walls
segments.body: The series presents the Doge’s Palace as a centre of government and surveillance, not simply a grand residence. It also explores the prison below it, the escape of Casanova, Venice’s changing fortunes and the building’s later transformation into a tourist destination.

At Versailles and Blenheim, the programme turns to monarchy, family life and the architecture of power. Its final stop is Ludwig II’s Neuschwanstein, a castle shaped by Romanticism and Wagner, whose builder’s death in a nearby lake remains unexplained.

content.headline: The Witch Farm turns Danny Robins’s paranormal podcast into drama
content.shortHeadline: The Witch Farm brings a real-life haunting to TV
content.standfirst: Robins’s drama adapts his podcast account of a family’s unsettling experiences in the Welsh countryside. He says the story leaves room for uncertainty, rather than claiming to prove that ghosts are real.

image.caption: Danny Robins, creator of The Witch Farm and host of the Uncanny podcast.

sources.originalTitle: Danny Robins: ‘My wife has never listened to Uncanny. She finds it terrifying’

segments.body: The Witch Farm is a four-part BBC drama inspired by accounts of a family’s experiences at a remote Welsh farmhouse between 1989 and 1996. Its story follows Bill, his pregnant partner Liz and his teenage son as unsettling events make them question whether they are alone.

segments.title: Holding space for doubt
segments.body: Danny Robins, whose podcast investigated the case, says he does not consider himself a believer. He describes his approach as one that takes people’s accounts seriously without turning them into proof of the supernatural, including when witnesses may be dealing with difficult personal circumstances.

Robins traces his interest in the unexplained to childhood, when ghost stories left room for uncertainty. He thinks today’s children are more often given fully explained fictional worlds, though he acknowledges that the question of what lies beyond death is partly personal.

content.headline: Russell Brand documentary Open Secret examines an industry’s complicity
content.shortHeadline: Open Secret examines how Russell Brand’s behaviour was enabled
content.standfirst: The documentary combines testimony from people in Brand’s orbit with footage of his public persona and the reporting that led to his conviction. The review argues that its most disturbing point is how often his behaviour was visible and excused.

image.caption: Russell Brand in the Netflix documentary Open Secret.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Russell Brand documentary feels like a horror film

segments.body: Open Secret follows the reporting by Sunday Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace and includes interviews with comedians, writers and former partners. The review notes that Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault and has begun serving a prison sentence.

segments.title: What was allowed in public
segments.body: The reviewer says the film’s force comes from setting accounts of harm alongside footage of Brand’s celebrity years, when sexualised jokes and boundary-crossing behaviour were often treated as part of his public image. Some testimony is attributed to women describing alleged abuse; the article distinguishes those accounts from the convictions.

The review argues that Brand’s conduct was enabled by a wider culture that valued the “bad boy” persona and left people who wanted to speak out fearing they would not be believed. It sees the documentary’s central indictment as extending beyond one individual to the institutions and audiences that tolerated him.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future follows years of creative and commercial strain
content.shortHeadline: What went wrong for Doctor Who—and what could bring it back?
content.standfirst: The BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special and ended its partnership with Disney+, leaving the long-running series without a current Doctor or confirmed next step. Fans and writers differ on whether it needs a pause, new backing or simply a return to television.

image.caption: Illustrations of several actors who have played Doctor Who.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off air since its 2025 series, starring Ncuti Gatwa, and the BBC has cancelled a planned Christmas special. The broadcaster has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and is seeking a new partner to help fund future production, but none has yet been announced.

segments.title: A series built to change
segments.body: The feature traces the programme’s revivals and repeated changes of lead actor and showrunner. Some fans argue the latest scripts became harder to follow; others point to the show’s long tradition of reinvention as a reason it can return.

Comedian Frank Skinner says he does not understand why the BBC has kept the show off air for so long, while writer Mark Gatiss has suggested a break may be appropriate. No decision on a new Doctor or production partner is reported.

content.headline: I’m a Celebrity row over AJ Odudu’s ‘aggressive’ label prompts debate
content.shortHeadline: An I’m a Celebrity exchange reignites debate over stereotyping
content.standfirst: A reviewer argues that Mariella Frostrup’s description of AJ Odudu as “aggressive” echoed a familiar stereotype about Black women. The article reports that fellow campmates disagreed with Frostrup’s reading of the exchange.

image.caption: AJ Odudu in I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!

sources.originalTitle: Mariella Frostrup’s behaviour is all too familiar to Black women like me

segments.body: On I’m a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here!, AJ Odudu challenged Mariella Frostrup after Frostrup rebuffed her offer to help with cooking. Frostrup called Odudu’s response “aggressive”; the reviewer argues that the exchange did not support that description.

segments.title: A loaded description
segments.body: The writer connects the label to a recurring experience for Black women, whose reasonable disagreement can be misread as aggression. The article says Wayne Rooney and Claire Sweeney, who witnessed the exchange, disagreed with Frostrup’s account.

The piece reports that producers had spoken to Frostrup about her language. Although the two women later tried to clear the air, the reviewer says Frostrup did not retract the word, leaving the disagreement unresolved.

content.headline: GTA VI makes everyday routines part of its criminal-world appeal
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI finds unexpected pleasure in everyday routines
content.standfirst: The game’s chores, shopping and care for a pet snake can feel as absorbing as its robberies and car chases. A review essay argues that Rockstar makes routine satisfying by giving players a home and relationships to care about.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI pairs crime with the everyday business of keeping house.

sources.originalTitle: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine

segments.body: In Grand Theft Auto VI, Jason’s daily tasks include working out, choosing clothes, feeding his pet snake and fixing things around his apartment. The essay finds these routines unexpectedly compelling amid the game’s crime and constant demands from friends and employers.

segments.title: Routine with a reason
segments.body: The writer argues that many games already revolve around completing tasks efficiently, but GTA VI makes those actions pleasurable through its detailed world and tactile feedback. The difference, the essay suggests, is the relationship between Jason and Lucia: daily tasks feel meaningful because the characters depend on one another.

content.headline: GTA VI’s classical radio station pairs Yuja Wang with virtual crime
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s classical station makes Tchaikovsky part of the chaos
content.standfirst: Pianist Yuja Wang hosts Symphony FM in Grand Theft Auto VI, choosing 16 classical works for a world of heists, driving and romance. The review sees the station as an entertaining way to introduce a vast audience to unfamiliar musical worlds.

image.caption: Grand Theft Auto VI, where Yuja Wang hosts a classical music station.

sources.originalTitle: Steal a chopper listening to Liszt! I love how Grand Theft Auto VI went crazy for classical

segments.body: Symphony FM is hosted in the game by real-life pianist Yuja Wang, who selected 16 works for the station. The playlist includes her performances of Ravel and Prokofiev, alongside pieces by composers including Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Sibelius and Mahler.

segments.title: A different soundtrack for the sandbox
segments.body: The essay describes how the classical pieces accompany everything from driving and romance to robberies and violence. Wang’s scripted comments make jokes about classical music’s reputation, while the review argues that the station offers players a route into music beyond the game’s more expected sounds.

The reviewer notes that listeners may debate the choices and catches a mismatch between one spoken introduction and the piece that follows. Even so, the essay sees the station’s scale and reach as an unusual opportunity for classical music within a popular game.

content.headline: Few women reviewed GTA VI, despite its first female lead in decades
content.shortHeadline: Why so few women reviewed GTA VI
content.standfirst: The review count for Grand Theft Auto VI included only six women among 156 critics, according to the article. It argues that this imbalance reflects the wider scarcity and precarity of women in games journalism, as well as a missed chance to hear more perspectives on Lucia.

image.caption: Lucia Caminos, one of the central characters in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?

segments.body: When the review embargo lifted, only six of 156 critics appeared to be women, the article reports. It also cites a survey of editorial teams at major games sites, finding that women made up just over a quarter of the writers counted.

segments.title: A narrow range of voices
segments.body: The writer connects the numbers to media consolidation, job losses, burnout and the particular hostility directed at women, queer and non-white critics. The absence is especially striking, the article argues, because Lucia is the first central female protagonist in the main GTA series in 30 years.

The piece asks what female critics might have brought to discussion of Lucia’s story and the game’s treatment of gender and contemporary America. It leaves open whether the wider audience for GTA VI will lead to more diverse critical coverage in the future.

content.headline: Satellite shorelines reveal metre-scale differences in beach tides
content.shortHeadline: Satellite images reveal sharp differences in beach tides
content.standfirst: A study of 40 years of Pacific shoreline images found tidal heights can vary substantially along a single beach. Mapping those local differences could help improve tide and flood forecasts, especially where gauges are scarce.

image.caption: Satellite measurements found tidal heights differed by almost a metre across a beach in New Zealand.

sources.originalTitle: How a new way of measuring tides could make flood forecasts more accurate

segments.body: Researchers used satellite photographs of shorelines as a measure of tidal height, estimating levels every 100 metres. Existing tide gauges record conditions at a particular spot, while satellite radar measurements typically average across much larger areas.

segments.title: A more local picture
segments.body: The analysis found differences of almost a metre across New Zealand’s South Taranaki Bight, a 90km bay. Such variation could mean neighbouring areas face different flood risks during the same storm. The researchers say the method could help make forecasts more local, but the reporting does not establish that it has yet improved operational warnings.

content.headline: China sends its first foreign astronaut to the Tiangong space station
content.shortHeadline: Pakistan’s first astronaut reaches China’s Tiangong station
content.standfirst: Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali has joined the crew of China’s Tiangong station, a first for the programme as Beijing seeks international partners. He will carry out experiments before returning earlier than the usual six-month rotation.

image.caption: The Shenzhou 24 crew, including Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali.

sources.originalTitle: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations

segments.body: Ali, a Pakistani air force pilot and payload specialist, reached Tiangong aboard Shenzhou 24. China says the flight begins the internationalisation of its space operations. Ali is the first Pakistani to reach orbit and the first foreign astronaut to visit the Chinese station.

segments.title: A shorter mission
segments.body: Ali is due to conduct experiments on microalgae as a potential food source and on how spaceflight affects quinoa seeds. Unlike the usual six-month Tiangong rotation, he will return with two members of the previous crew. China has also launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover is expected to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

segments.title: A bid for partners
segments.body: Space consultant Blaine Curcio told the Guardian that flying another country’s astronaut is a major undertaking and could help make China’s station a more attractive partner. The article notes that China is seeking cooperation as the International Space Station approaches its planned retirement from 2030; the future of any replacement remains uncertain.

content.headline: Dolphins with stable social groups tend to live longer, study finds
content.shortHeadline: Long-term dolphin friendships linked with longer lives
content.standfirst: Researchers tracked Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Western Australia for nearly 40 years and found that those maintaining stronger, more stable social groups tended to live longer. The study describes an association, not proof that social ties cause longevity.

image.caption: Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins in Shark Bay, Western Australia.

sources.originalTitle: Dolphins with active social lives and big friendship groups live longer, Australian researchers discover

segments.body: The study drew on tens of thousands of observations of individually identifiable dolphins in Shark Bay. Researchers found that dolphins with the strongest and most stable social groups tended to live longest. Their group sizes and social preferences changed with age, and males generally spent time in larger groups than females.

segments.title: Social ties have trade-offs
segments.body: Socialising can help dolphins form bonds, share information and find mates, but it may also bring stress and increase the spread of disease. The researchers said long-term observations helped them see how social preferences vary between individuals. An outside cetacean researcher described the findings as another demonstration of the complexity of dolphin behaviour.

content.headline: Warming winters put Wisconsin’s cranberry harvest at risk
content.shortHeadline: Cranberry growers race to adapt to warmer, erratic weather
content.standfirst: Heat, heavy rain and unstable winter conditions are putting pressure on US cranberry farms. Researchers and growers are testing more resilient varieties and using tools including AI and drones to adapt, though the reporting does not quantify how effective those approaches will be.

image.caption: Workers harvest cranberries at a farm in New Jersey.

sources.originalTitle: Cranberry jam: warming winters and extreme weather threaten a traditional holiday fruit

segments.body: Cranberry growers face different climate pressures across the US. Heatwaves can scald fruit on the vine, while humid conditions and heavy rain can encourage crop rot. In Wisconsin, warmer winters can bring premature thaws that melt protective ice on the vines before a sudden freeze.

segments.title: Adapting the crop
segments.body: Researchers and growers are working to identify and breed varieties better able to withstand extreme weather and disease. Farms are also using drones to apply fertiliser and monitor temperatures. The reporting describes these as adaptation efforts under way, not proven solutions to the changing conditions.

content.headline: US Army detonates ageing lead azide stockpile in Iowa
content.shortHeadline: Lead azide stockpile detonated at Iowa ammunition plant
content.standfirst: The Army detonated about 9,700 pounds of unstable lead azide at its Iowa ammunition plant on 25 November. The reporting outlines steps intended to limit lead pollution, but does not report post-blast monitoring results or the extent of any release.

sources.originalTitle: Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa

segments.body: The Army detonated 68 drums containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Officials said crystallisation on the ageing barrels made it too risky to open them for chemical treatment, and that leaving the material in place carried a risk of an uncontrolled explosion.

segments.title: Pollution risk remains
segments.body: Before the detonation, the Army said its containment measures were intended to limit lead dust, which modelling suggested could travel as far as 100 miles. Local authorities advised people in potentially affected areas to stay indoors and reduce outside air circulation. The court allowed the blast to proceed after rejecting an emergency request to stop it; the article does not say what post-event testing found.

segments.title: Monitoring urged
segments.body: The Army said water tanks, foam and other barriers would help capture particulate matter. Experts quoted in the report differed in emphasis: one expected no observable acute clinical signs and described the overall risk as minimal, while another warned that the blast would spread lead and said monitoring the site and surrounding areas would be important.

content.headline: Huawei convicted on 10 counts in US trade secrets and fraud case
content.shortHeadline: Huawei convicted of trade secrets theft and fraud in US trial
content.standfirst: A Brooklyn jury found the Chinese telecoms company guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but acquitted it of racketeering. Huawei says it will challenge the verdict; sentencing is planned for 2027.

image.caption: Huawei defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Brooklyn trial.

sources.originalTitle: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
China’s Huawei convicted of stealing US trade secrets
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets

segments.body: After a two-month trial, jurors found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and conspiracy to violate US sanctions. They rejected the more serious racketeering charge, which alleged the company operated as a criminal enterprise. Sentencing is planned for September 2027.

segments.title: A long-running case
segments.body: Prosecutors presented allegations involving technology from rival companies and Huawei’s business in Iran. The case began with US charges announced in 2019, following the arrest of Huawei finance chief Meng Wanzhou in Canada. She later returned to China under a deal with US prosecutors; charges against her were dropped.

segments.title: The company plans to fight
segments.body: Huawei says the charges it was convicted of lack legal merit and that it will take necessary legal action. Its defence lawyer told the BBC the company was gratified by the racketeering acquittal but had mixed feelings about the rest of the verdict and expected to appeal.

perspectives.body: Huawei’s defence argued that prosecutors had built their case around treating the company as a criminal organisation. Its lawyer said the jury’s rejection of the racketeering count was significant, while maintaining Huawei deserved acquittals on all counts.

content.headline: UK battery subsidy shortlist raises security concerns over Chinese technology
content.shortHeadline: UK battery subsidy shortlist draws scrutiny over Chinese links
content.standfirst: Projects using Chinese-made lithium-ion batteries dominate a provisional shortlist for UK energy-storage support. Critics say the cost-focused assessment gives too little weight to security risks over the lifetime of the projects; Ofgem says it is considering consultation responses.

image.caption: Lithium-ion batteries dominate the UK regulator’s provisional shortlist for storage support.

sources.originalTitle: China-linked battery projects could receive UK funding despite security warnings

segments.body: Eleven of the 16 projects shortlisted for a UK long-duration energy-storage scheme rely on lithium-ion batteries, which are typically made in China and operated with Chinese software. The regulator Ofgem is expected to confirm which projects will receive support in the coming weeks.

segments.title: Cost versus resilience
segments.body: Industry sources say Ofgem’s assessment gives substantial weight to cost and does not specifically assess the risk of security breaches over the projects’ full lifetimes. British vanadium-flow battery maker Invinity said it may reconsider UK manufacturing plans after only one project using its technology made the shortlist. Ofgem says it assessed proposals against the government’s legal and policy framework.

segments.title: Companies respond
segments.body: Developers Field Energy and Statera Energy have links to Chinese battery suppliers. Both say they take security seriously and comply with national guidance. The government says it is working to build secure, resilient supply chains; the final subsidy decisions have not yet been announced.

content.headline: Microsoft sets ‘Code Red’ after major Outlook outage exposed recovery gaps
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft launches ‘Code Red’ response to Outlook outage
content.standfirst: After an outage disrupted Microsoft 365 services for almost a day, the company is prioritising faster recovery and improved traffic management. Reporting also describes fragmented internal communications during the incident; the changes are plans, not evidence that future failures will be prevented.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
